body.text: The controversial and ongoing Intensive Special Revision (SIR) in India, which has been tied to citizenship, unlike the passport and other documents, is reported to have already struck almost 13.3 crore names off the electoral rolls. This means that around one out of ten people in India either do not exist or cannot automatically claim citizenship. It is arguably the most sweeping deregistration of putative or extant citizens anywhere in the world, but we need to add to it similar numbers globally, where there are around 38 million refugees and another 67 million internally displaced persons, whose citizenship is always fraught. By conservative estimates.

Similar trends of denying or revoking citizenship have existed throughout the century of “nationalisms”—that is, the 20th century. Most obviously, one thinks of German Jews in Nazi Germany, or the Nakba in 1948, during which Zionists dislocated and excluded about a million Palestinians from the territorial space of what is now Israel. But the tempo seems to have picked up in the 21st century.

The two writers of this essay come into this disturbing tradition from different trajectories. Tabish Khair was born in a town in Bihar, not far from the ancestral village where his ancestors had lived for at least a few centuries. Travelling on an Indian passport, until the confusion of SIR, he had taken his (Indian) citizenship for granted, despite being away from the nation for almost 30 years.

But when Sebastien Doubinsky’s father was born in Paris, in 1934, he was born stateless, as his father, Jacques (Yacob) Doubinsky, had arrived as an immigrant in 1924. Jewish, Ukrainian (Russian at the time), anarchist, he was not welcome and was on police watch. He finally obtained his nationality in 1945 because he had been an active member of the Résistance (against the Nazi occupation of France). Sebastien, therefore, holds that he is, in many ways, French by chance, just as his grandfather had arrived in France by chance. Today, there are millions of individuals who are in the same situation as both his grandfather and his father, nationless, while flags and dotted borderlines are rising everywhere. Then there are increasing numbers being rendered stateless using new bureaucratic measures, such as SIR in India, a process probably soon to be aided by Artificial Intelligence.

This trend is not confined to the non-West or economically fraught nations. In Denmark, where Sebastien and Tabish both live, it is nearly impossible for non-Western immigrants to obtain Danish nationality, and it is a trend one finds in many European and economically developed countries. The refugees and immigrants are thus placed in an administrative buffer zone, in which “neither, nor” becomes the defining norm and the central argument of racism/xenophobia-fuelled political parties.

The “Western” paradox, of course, is that most of these immigrants and refugees are arriving because of conflicts and political turmoil largely caused or kindled by Western countries. All this is heavily documented, and only hypocrites and populists continue to deny this factual reality. But there is another paradox that, in our opinion, flies under the radar: what, exactly, defines this virtue of the West that is so difficult for these immigrants and refugees to obtain? The first and most common argument we hear is “democratic values”—but in what sense? We are told, from our first school year on, that democracy is fragile, that you have to learn about it, that it is a complex process, etc.

Does that mean that democracy can be only understood by, say, white or at least affluent people? Does it imply that religious, political refugees or, more simply, poor foreign people of the wrong skin colour can never attain a sufficient level of subtlety, education, or intelligence in order to participate in Western “democratic” systems? Does it mean that we are not-so-symbolically enacting Aldous Huxley’s eugenicist Brave New World vision of a world where the happiness of the few is based on a genetically determined social asymmetry?

Statelessness has become, since the late 1980s, an equivalent of inferiority, of a lack of moral values, of an impossibility of integrating, precisely, a “state”, understood as a culturally essentialized entity. The irony is that statelessness is not seen as the same problem between all minorities: for instance, in this part of Europe, Ukrainians are more welcome than Palestinians or Syrians, creating pockets of “integrationability” within our system, deeply rooted in colonial traditions and racialist theories. By doing this, Western states, ironically, dismantle the very foundation of our democracies: the fundamental right of existing as equals, different but equal, opening thus to the core question: are our states still democracies, if they cannot accept to integrate stateless people?

Interestingly, the way SIR is being conducted in India seems to replicate a similar process, using just different adjectives. Then there are two differing examples in, until recently, the oil-rich and hence flourishing Middle East. We have Israel, which denies citizenship even to people (apart from a token handful) whose families lived on its territories as late as 1948, and sometimes later, while extending it to people from Europe or America who claim to belong to a specific religion. Against, or parallel to it, are nations like the UAE, the until-recently flourishing Arab monarchies, which technically allow you semi-citizenship as long as you can afford it. In both cases, however, statelessness is either created or remains a prospect.

The state, democratic or not, has come to wield citizenship as a powerful weapon—either carrot or stick, or both!—and statelessness of various kinds is being spawned as a result. This is, in different dimensions, a global problem—but there is no effective global opposition to it. The numbers of the nationless are likely to increase in the 21st century, and genocides, as we know from history, are always connected to nationlessness. It is already happening.

Seb Doubinsky is an associate professor in the French department of Aarhus University and a bilingual French writer. Tabish Khair is an Indian novelist and associate professor in the English department of Aarhus University.
